title: Bridget of Sweden (1303–1373)
hook: mother of eight, widow, founder, co-patron of Europe

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Western Schism: rival popes, and sincere people, saints among them, on different sides. Your line was even saints were confused.

A fresh grave at a monastery in Sweden. The widow standing beside it was married young. She has raised a houseful of children, run an estate, served at the royal court, and walked a long pilgrimage road beside her husband, Ulf. Now Ulf is buried, and the life she knew is over. The expected next chapter is a quiet one: a chair by the fire, grandchildren, prayers. Instead, she begins again, in a new country, with a new work and a voice that reaches popes.
screen: `A GRAVE IN SWEDEN.` → `A HOUSEFUL OF CHILDREN, NOW GROWN.` → `SHE BEGINS AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Start with the first life. Bridget was born into a noble family and married young. Tradition remembers her as a mother who prayed with her children and fed the poor at her own door, and one of her daughters, Catherine, is honored as a saint too. Next, the turn. After Ulf died, Bridget gave away much of what she had and gave herself to prayer. She wrote down visions, later gathered as her Revelations, many of them meditations on the suffering of Christ. The Church is careful here. The Catechism says private revelations don't add to the faith; they can help people live it, and they're weighed, not required. Then, the new work. Bridget founded the Order of the Most Holy Savior, under a rule she wrote. And she went to Rome, and stayed. The popes of her day lived at Avignon, in France, and Bridget, years before Catherine of Siena, wrote to them plainly, urging them home to Rome. She didn't live to see it settled; yesterday's schism came after her. Finally, Europe. The Church has named Bridget a co-patron of Europe, beside Catherine of Siena and Edith Stein. A woman who crossed the continent on pilgrim roads, from the far north to Rome and on to the Holy Land, now stands for the whole of it. Paul's first letter to Timothy describes a widow who trusts in God and keeps praying, night and day. Bridget did that, then got up and went to work. A second life can be larger than the first.
screen: `A NOBLE WIFE AND MOTHER.` · `WIDOWED, SHE GIVES HERSELF TO PRAYER.` · `AN ORDER FOUNDED, A LIFE IN ROME.` · `A CO-PATRON OF EUROPE.` · then, large: `A WIDOW'S SECOND LIFE.`

segments.voice: Picture the roads Bridget walked, north to south, cold coasts, mountain passes, crowded cities, or one country in Europe you know or have family in, and let a few faces come: a family just arrived somewhere new, a parish choir, a teenager on a night train. If you pray, ask Bridget's prayers for them or pray an Our Father with that place in mind; if not, hold it the way you'd hold a friend's name.
Bridget. A noble wife and mother who, once widowed, founded an order, moved to Rome, and spoke plainly to popes. Today's word.
Your line: a widow's second life. Loss closed one door for Bridget, and she walked through another. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Bridget's feast in the calendar, and the order she founded, the Bridgettines, still lives and prays in houses in several countries. Some Catholics pray for Europe on her feast and on the feasts of its other patron saints.

notes: The index hook says 'mother of eight'; under the claims rule no number is stated in the voice ('a houseful of children'). Confirm the count if the Keeper wants it restored with a source.

Biographical facts to confirm: noble birth, married young to Ulf Gudmarsson, service at the Swedish royal court, pilgrimage with Ulf (to Santiago de Compostela) before his death, daughter Saint Catherine of Sweden, founding of the Order of the Most Holy Savior under her own rule, life in Rome, letters urging the popes to return from Avignon, pilgrimage to the Holy Land, death in Rome before the papacy's settled return and before the Western Schism.
'Tradition remembers her as a mother who prayed with her children and fed the poor at her own door': attributed, confirm acceptable.
CCC 67 paraphrased: private revelations do not belong to the deposit of faith and do not improve or complete Christ's revelation, but can help people live it more fully.
Co-patron of Europe with Catherine of Siena and Edith Stein (Teresa Benedicta of the Cross), per John Paul II's Spes Aedificandi; date omitted under the claims rule.
1 Timothy 5:5 paraphrased rather than quoted (Douay-Rheims wording not verified).
